skill.name: analysis-tshark
skill.description: Analyze authorized packet captures and live network traffic with TShark for incident response, protocol inspection, forensic extraction, and security monitoring.
skill.summary: Capture, filter, inspect, and report network traffic with TShark.
skill.author: AgentSecOps

security_audit.summary: Most static alerts are false positives caused by Markdown formatting, defensive examples, offline packet filters, and framework terminology. Confirmed risks include remote pipe-to-shell installation, mutable third-party token exposure, privileged packet capture, and TLS key handling. Credential extraction and packet-metadata email alerts add sensitive-data exposure.

remediation.issue: The CI template pipes a remote script from a mutable branch directly to bash.
remediation.suggestion: Pin tfsec to a reviewed release, download it separately, verify its checksum or signature, and execute only after validation.

remediation.issue: A mutable third-party action receives GITHUB_TOKEN.
remediation.suggestion: Pin the action to a reviewed commit SHA and reduce job permissions to the minimum required for the scan.

remediation.issue: Many live-capture examples run the full TShark process with sudo.
remediation.suggestion: Require confirmation before live capture and prefer narrowly scoped dumpcap permissions or capabilities over running TShark as root.

remediation.issue: Credential, POST-body, NTLM, TLS-key, and private-key workflows handle highly sensitive data.
remediation.suggestion: Add mandatory redaction, encrypted storage, access logging, retention limits, and secure deletion steps beside every extraction workflow.

remediation.issue: The monitoring script emails packet-derived metadata.
remediation.suggestion: Require an approved internal destination, minimize alert fields, protect mail transport, and prevent raw credentials or payloads from entering messages.

semantic_findings.title: Credential and Authentication Artifact Extraction
semantic_findings.description: The guide instructs users to extract plaintext credentials, NTLM responses, HTTP POST bodies, and authentication data from captures. These dual-use workflows can expose reusable secrets and personal data if authorization or storage controls fail.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The cited sections explicitly provide commands for credential extraction and writing POST data or NTLM responses to local files.

semantic_findings.title: Packet Metadata Disclosure Through Email Alerts
semantic_findings.description: The monitoring example emails packet-derived source, destination, host, and DNS data to a configured mailbox. This can disclose monitored network metadata through an external mail path.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The script pipes each TShark alert line into the mail command, and the selected fields include internal addresses, HTTP hosts, and DNS names.

content.value_statement: Packet captures are difficult to inspect quickly and consistently. This skill provides TShark workflows for filtering traffic, extracting evidence, and reporting findings.
actual_capabilities: Captures authorized network traffic with interface, duration, packet count, BPF, and ring-buffer controls.
Reads PCAP files and applies Wireshark display filters for HTTP, DNS, TLS, SMB, email, and wireless traffic.
Extracts protocol fields, transferred objects, authentication artifacts, conversations, endpoints, and forensic timelines.
Identifies beaconing, DNS tunneling, port scanning, large uploads, suspicious downloads, and failed connections.
Exports analysis as text, CSV, JSON, statistics, and incident indicators for downstream reporting.
limitations: TShark, Wireshark, and supporting command-line tools must be installed separately.
Live capture needs operating-system permissions and written authorization for the monitored network.
Encrypted payload analysis requires authorized TLS key logs or private keys.
Example filters require adaptation and do not independently confirm malicious activity.

use_cases.title: Triage an Incident Capture
use_cases.description: Filter a PCAP for suspicious hosts, protocols, failed connections, beaconing, and transferable incident indicators.

use_cases.title: Investigate Protocol Behavior
use_cases.description: Inspect DNS, HTTP, TLS, SMB, and authentication fields to diagnose application or network problems.

use_cases.title: Preserve Forensic Evidence
use_cases.description: Build a traffic timeline, extract authorized artifacts, document scope, and maintain defensible evidence handling.

prompt_templates.title: Summarize a PCAP
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze [capture path] with TShark. Summarize protocols, endpoints, conversations, errors, and notable traffic without extracting sensitive payloads.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner overview of an existing capture

prompt_templates.title: Build a Display Filter
prompt_templates.prompt: Create and explain a TShark display filter for [protocol or behavior] in [capture path]. Show expected fields and interpretation limits.

prompt_templates.title: Triage Suspicious Traffic
prompt_templates.prompt: Triage [capture path] for [incident indicators]. Correlate timestamps, hosts, DNS, HTTP, TLS, and connection patterns. Return prioritized findings with evidence.

prompt_templates.title: Design an Authorized Capture Workflow
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a least-privilege TShark workflow for [approved scope]. Include capture filters, rotation, evidence protection, validation, retention, and cleanup requirements.

output_examples.input: Summarize the main traffic in incident.pcap.
output: Primary protocols: DNS, TLS, HTTP, and SMB.
Most active endpoint pair: workstation to application server.
Notable event: repeated DNS queries at regular intervals require investigation.

output_examples.input: Find large HTTP uploads and explain the evidence.
output_examples.output: Three POST requests exceed the selected threshold. The report lists timestamps, source and destination hosts, content lengths, and validation caveats.

output_examples.input: Create a forensic review plan for a wireless capture.
output_examples.output: The plan covers authorization, SSID and client inventory, deauthentication checks, handshake review, evidence hashing, access controls, and secure deletion.

best_practices: Confirm written authorization, capture scope, retention, and privacy requirements before accessing traffic.
Use narrow capture filters, short durations, least privilege, encrypted storage, and strict evidence access controls.
Corroborate packet indicators with logs, asset context, and timelines before declaring malicious activity.
anti_patterns: Do not capture networks, interfaces, credentials, or wireless traffic outside an explicitly approved scope.
Do not store PCAP files, decrypted payloads, passwords, hashes, or key material in plaintext or shared locations.
Do not execute remote installation scripts, unverified filters, or privileged commands without reviewing their source and impact.

faq.question: Does this skill install TShark?
faq.answer: No. Install TShark or Wireshark through a trusted package source before using the workflows.

faq.question: Can it analyze an existing PCAP without root access?
faq.answer: Usually yes. Reading an accessible capture file generally does not require live-capture privileges.

faq.question: Why can live capture require elevated permissions?
faq.answer: Packet capture needs raw network access. Prefer narrowly assigned capture capabilities instead of running the complete analyzer as root.

faq.question: Can it decrypt TLS traffic?
faq.answer: Yes, when authorized session secrets or suitable private keys are available. Those secrets require strict protection and deletion controls.

faq.question: Does a suspicious filter match prove an attack?
faq.answer: No. Filters identify evidence for review. Confirm findings with host logs, asset roles, expected behavior, and additional telemetry.

faq.question: How should capture files be shared?
faq.answer: Minimize and redact sensitive fields, encrypt transfers, restrict recipients, preserve integrity, and follow the approved retention policy.
